page_title: Let's code a TCP/IP stack, 2: IPv4 & ICMPv4

summary.title: Let's code a TCP/IP stack, 2: IPv4 & ICMPv4
summary.one_liner: You learn the IPv4 and ICMPv4 header layouts and how the Internet checksum is computed and verified, then build a minimal IP layer that answers ICMP echo requests (pings) in a userspace TCP/IP stack.
takeaways: IPv4 header fields (version, IHL, TOS, length, id, flags, fragment offset, TTL, protocol, checksum, source and destination addresses) and their purpose.
How the Internet checksum is computed as the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum, and how to verify it (result 0 means likely good).
ICMPv4 message types (Echo Request 8, Echo Reply 0, Destination Unreachable 3) and the echo id/seq fields used for pinging.
IP is connectionless and unreliable, so reliability must come from higher layers such as TCP; fragmentation is left as an exercise.
summary.summary: This tutorial is part of a series building a userspace TCP/IP stack in C-style code. It explains the IPv4 header fields as a C struct, including length, TTL, protocol, and fragmentation-related fields, and why IP is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery. It walks through the Internet checksum with a worked example header, then covers the ICMPv4 header, the echo request/reply and destination unreachable formats, and how to test the stack with pings from a shell. Options, fragmentation, and IPv6 are deliberately left out or mentioned as future work.
